adjudication_label: batch_2:thermal stability and dissolution of oxide phases
canonical_question: Does the high thermal stability of the oxides mean they are stable up to 1300°C, or could they dissolve partially during the SPS process despite the claim?

question_variants.question: Does the high thermal stability of the oxides mean they are stable up to 1300°C, or could they dissolve partially during the SPS process despite the claim?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The text claims high thermal stability and states they were not dissolved during the SPS process at 1300°C. It does not provide specific data on whether partial dissolution might occur at higher temperatures or under different SPS conditions, relying on the general claim of 'very high' stability.

answers.answer: The text states the oxides have 'very high' thermal stability and were 'not dissolved during the SPS process' (which was conducted at 1300°C). It does not provide specific data on stability up to 1300°C versus higher temperatures or partial dissolution behavior.
answers.boundary_limitation: No data on behavior above 1300°C or partial dissolution.
evidence_spans: MA powder prepared from the elemental powders (granularity −325 mesh) by high energy ball milling in an Ar atmosphere for 42 h using tungsten carbide balls.
The mean particle size of the MA powder was ≈3 μm and MA particles consisted of nanocrystalline grains
MA and AT powders were compacted by SPS in an SPS 10-4 device (Santa Rosa, California, CA, USA) using a graphite die (Ø 20 mm) and punches to compact the powder using pressure of 80 MPa.

source_evidence_spans: The thermal stability of these oxides is very high and therefore they were not dissolved during the SPS process [ [43] ]
